cards.title: Constant-factor Π₂ hardness of approximating linear discrepancy
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Historical conjecture, resolved affirmatively: is there an absolute constant γ>1 such that distinguishing lindisc(A)≤t from lindisc(A)>γt is Π₂^P-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, given a rational m×n matrix A and a positive rational threshold t? Here lindisc(A)=max_{w∈[0,1]ⁿ} min_{x∈{0,1}ⁿ} ‖A(w−x)‖∞. Manurangsi’s published theorem establishes the requested hardness for every fixed γ=9/8−ε with 0<ε<1/8. The source’s damaged fraction 32 referred to a 3/2 covering-radius comparison; its conjecture asks for analogous constant-factor hardness of linear discrepancy, not explicitly the identical 3/2 factor.
cards.why: Establishes that approximating the worst-case error of binary rounding captures the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy, beyond ordinary NP-hardness.

cards.definitions: The matrix entries and t are encoded as binary rational numerators and positive denominators; both dimensions are part of the input and unbounded. For y∈Rᵐ, ‖y‖∞=max_{j∈[m]}|y_j|. A fractional vector w ranges over the entire real cube [0,1]ⁿ and x is a binary rounding of all its coordinates. Thus the maximization is outside the minimization: a different x may be chosen for each w. The maximum exists because the minimum of finitely many continuous functions of w is continuous on a compact set. This is not discrepancy at just w=(1/2,…,1/2), and the rounding vector does not range over all integer vectors as in lattice covering radius. The promise problem accepts instances with lindisc(A)≤t and rejects those with lindisc(A)>γt; behavior in the intervening gap is unrestricted. Π₂^P consists of languages decidable by a polynomial-time predicate with one polynomial-length universal binary quantifier followed by one polynomial-length existential binary quantifier. Hardness means that every language in this class has a deterministic polynomial-time map taking its yes instances into the low-discrepancy case and its no instances into the high-discrepancy case. The factor γ is fixed before the reduction and does not depend on the matrix dimensions. A γ-approximation to the value in the one-sided convention returns v with lindisc(A)≤v≤γ lindisc(A); the gap statement avoids ambiguity about approximation conventions.
cards.answer_criterion: The published Π₂ reduction resolves the constant-factor hardness conjecture: it has lindisc(A)≤4/3 in the yes case and lindisc(A)≥3/2 in the no case, giving hardness at every factor strictly below 9/8. This is an unconditional hardness theorem, not an unconditional proof that no polynomial-time algorithm exists. It does not establish hardness at factor 3/2, and no such stronger target is substituted for the source’s general conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Worst-case rounding error is the quantity being approximated
context_blocks.text: Linear discrepancy measures the largest, over fractional vectors, of the smallest achievable row-wise rounding error. Finding a useful rounding for one given vector and estimating this worst-case value are different computational tasks.

context_blocks.title: The source’s hardness question had a later direct answer
context_blocks.text: Li and Nikolov proved NP-hardness of exact evaluation and membership of the rational threshold problem in Π₂. They conjectured analogous constant-factor Π₂ approximation hardness to the lattice covering-radius problem. Manurangsi’s 2021 theorem explicitly answers that question.

context_blocks.title: The numerical factors belong to different problems

Its reduction has thresholds 4/3 and 3/2, whose ratio is 9/8; the occurrence of 3/2 as an absolute no-case threshold must not be mistaken for that approximation ratio.
